preamble: The shift from 'ts' to 'ch' (tʃ) is a classic example of palatalization, where an alveolar affricate moves to a post-alveolar position, often triggered by following high vowels or palatal glides. Guaymí and Guatuso (Chibchan) changed Proto-Chibchan *ʦ to ʧ in all positions.

languageExamples.language: Proto-Muskogean to Eastern Muskogean (Alabama, Koasati, Creek, Mikasuki)

examples.to: Alabama and Koasati chinto, Creek cetto [tʃittoː], Mikasuki činti [tʃ]
examples.note: Follows Booker's reconstruction of *¢ [ts]; Haas reconstructed *c for this set, under which the eastern affricate would be the retention (Martin 2001). Western Choctaw sinti shows the opposite outcome *¢ > s.

examples.to: Alabama and Koasati nochi, Creek nucetv [notʃita]
Alabama and Koasati chakki, Creek cakketv
examples.note: Compare Choctaw and Chickasaw sakki. Before a consonant Alabama and Koasati show s instead (*ko¢tini 'wise' > kostini, *i¢katini 'small' > iskani), while Mikasuki keeps ičkani.

Other Mixean languages keep ts: Coatlán Mixe tzic, Totontepec tsic, Isthmus Mixe tsik; Zoquean Copainalá tzicu. Clark's Sayula orthography writes /tʃ/ as ch and /ts/ as ts, which are separate phonemes.
Totontepec mehʦk and Tlahuitoltepec mahʦk keep the alveolar affricate; Oluta has mesko.
*tz [ts] became ch before *a; before front vowels it stays ts, as in *lutzeʔ 'tongue' > ltseꞌ and *katzi 'be yellow' > Western Highland katsi²³.
